Application of Warm Isostatic Pressing to Densification of All Solid-State Composite Cathode 
Electrodes in All Solid-State Lithium-Ion Batteries 
 
Kazushi HAYASHI1*, Takuya MORI2, Kazunori FUKUDA2, Hiroyuki ITO3, and Yasuo MANABE3 
 
1Applied Physics Research Laboratory, Kobe Steel, Ltd., 1-5-5, Takatsukadai, Nishi-ku, Kobe, Hyogo 651-2271, Japan. 
2Kobelco Research Institute, Inc., 1-5-5, Takatsukadai, Nishi-ku, Kobe, Hyogo 651-2271, Japan.

Abstract  
All-solid-state batteries (ASSBs) have garnered significant attention for their potential use in high-performance Li-ion batteries for 
next-generation electric vehicles. Warm isostatic pressing (WIP) is a promising technique for the densification of ASSB electrodes. 
In this study, composite cathodes consisting of a mixture of Li(Ni1/3Mn1/3Co1/3)O2 and Li6PS5Cl were processed using WIP and 
assembled into test cells to investigate the correlation between the structure of the electrodes and their electrochemical performance. 
The structures of the electrodes were analyzed using X-ray computed tomography (CT) with synchrotron radiation at SPring-8. 
Electrochemical performance was evaluated through electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and charge-discharge measurements. 
The voids in the electrodes decreased as the WIP temperature increased, resulting in improved charge-discharge properties, which 
suggests a reduction in charge transfer resistance. Thus, WIP was found to be effective in the production of ASSBs. 
 
Keywords: Warm Isostatic Pressing (WIP), All-solid-state battery, Synchrotron X-ray computed tomography (CT), Electrochemical 
performance. 
 
Introduction 
With the strong demand for reducing CO2 emissions, all-solid-state batteries (ASSBs) have gained attention as an essential 
component for next-generation electric vehicles (EVs). ASSBs are expected to provide higher power, longer driving ranges, and 
enhanced safety for EVs. The development of solid electrolytes (SE) is a crucial issue1). Early research on achieving SEs with Li-ion 
conductivity equal to or greater than that of conventional liquid electrolytes. To date, promising SEs such as Li7P3S11, Li10GeP2S12, 
and argyrodite-type SEs (Li6PS5Cl and Li6PS5Br) have been identified in the literature2-6).  
To obtain superior charge-discharge properties, the application of SEs with high Li conductivity is the first step. In addition, 
controlling the interface between the active materials (AM) and SEs is particularly important because, unlike conventional Li-ion 
batteries, Li-ion conduction occurs only through the interface between the AM and SE7-9). Furthermore, densification of the 
electrodes is an essential process step not only for ensuring conformal contact but also achieving a higher specific power density 
sufficient for practical EV use. In pioneering work by Prof. Tatsumisago, it was shown that the relative density of 75Li2S-25P2S5 
exceeded 90% when compressed at pressures over 350 MPa10). As the density increased, the Li-ion conductivity of 75Li2S-25P2S5 
also increased with molding pressure, approaching bulk conductivity at 360 MPa. They also noted that dense pellets were obtained 
and small voids and cracks on the surface vanished when hot pressing at 200C due to treatment near the glass transition temperature. 
In the practical fabrication of ASSBs, both hot and cold isostatic pressing (HIP and CIP, respectively) are applicable for the 
densification of ASSB components due to their controllability and scalability11,12). However, there have been few reports on ASSBs 
using warm isostatic pressing (WIP), where densification is achieved through high pressure (~600 MPa) CIP at elevated 
temperatures13-15). Lee et al. reported ASSBs with a high energy density of over 900 Whl-1 by using WIP 13), stating that WIP 
improved the contact properties between the electrode and the electrolyte. The detailed densification mechanism remains unclear, and 
the effect of process pressure and temperature during WIP on the structure of the composite electrodes, and consequently on their 
electrochemical performance, is still an open question. Therefore, establishing a practical fabrication process for ASSBs is necessary. 
In this study, the structure of composite electrodes before and after WIP were examined using X-ray computed tomography (CT) 
with synchrotron radiation at SPring-8. Electrochemical characterization was also performed using electrochemical impedance 
spectroscopy and charge-discharge tests. The correlation between the microstructure of the composite cathodes and battery 
performance was investigated, providing insights for developing high-performance EVs equipped with ASSBs.  
 
Experiment 
A. Sample Preparation 
The AM used for the composite cathode was Li(Ni1/3Mn1/3Co1/3)O2, coated with LiNbO3. The SE consisted of Li6PS5Cl. These were 
mixed with a conductive agent of acetylene black, a binder, and a solvent to form a slurry with an electrode composition of 
74:23:3wt%. The slurry was coated onto Al foil, which served as the current collector, and then dried. The typical thickness of the 
fabricated composite electrodes was approximately 170 m. Finally, the electrodes were placed in laminate bags and vacuum-sealed.

WIP treatment was performed using a piston-type vertical CIP apparatus equipped with external sample heaters (Kobe Steel, Ltd.). 
The vessel was 80 mm in diameter and 180 mm in length. In this study, the process pressure was set at 600 MPa, while the process 
temperature was varied between room temperature (RT) and 190C (maximum temperature for the system) to examine the influence 
of the process temperature on the electrochemical performance of the electrodes. The pressurizing sequence was as follows: the 
pressure medium inside the vessel was heated. Once the medium reached the required temperature, the electrodes were loaded into 
the vessel at atmospheric pressure. The electrodes were then pressurized using the pressure medium and maintained at the process 
pressure, after which the pressure was released. The holding time was maintained at 1 min unless otherwise specified. The process 
duration refers to the holding time at the maximum pressure in each experiment. 
 
B. Structural Evaluation 
The structures of the composite electrodes before and after the WIP treatment were examined by X-ray CT using synchrotron 
radiation at SPring-8 (SUNBEAM: BL16B2). The incident X-ray beam was monochromatized and irradiated onto the samples at 30 
keV. The sample rotation angle during measurement was 180 and the exposure time was 4 s. CT data were obtained with Xsight 
Micron LC (Rigaku Innovative Technologies Europe) in every 0.1. The effective pixel size of the experimental setup was 0.65 µm. 
The CT samples were encapsulated in glass capillaries with a diameter of 0.8 mm, with Ar as the capillary atmosphere.  
Based on the CT values separately determined for the various components (AM, SE and voids/carbon), each voxel was classified into 
three categories to analyze the structure of the composite electrodes. Voids and carbon-related materials were not distinguished due 
to their high transparency to X-rays. Some samples were characterized by cross-sectional secondary electron microscopy (SEM). 
Elemental mapping was performed using energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscope (EDS). The cross-section was prepared by 
cryo-focused ion beam milling to avoid damage to the samples during preparation. 
 
C. Electrochemical Characterization 
The charge-discharge performance was examined using the test cell shown in Fig. 1. The test cells had a hybrid structure composed 
of the aforementioned composite electrode and a bulky pellet-type SE to extract the electrochemical performance of the composite 
electrodes for comparison. The working electrode was a composite electrode with and without WIP treatment. The SE was a pellet 
consisting of Li6PS5Cl formed by uniaxial press at 600 MPa. An In-Li alloy was used as the counter electrode. The effective cell area 
was approximately 1 cm2, and the thickness of the pellet SE was 600 m. The measurements were carried out under a confining 
pressure of 150 MPa to maintain contact between the components. 
The charge-discharge performance was evaluated at a rate of 0.1 C with constant current (CC) mode for discharging and both CC and 
constant voltage (CV) modes for charging. The CV conditions for charging were 3.68 V for 1 h, and the cutoff voltage for 
discharging was set to 2.48 V. The total number of cycles for the charge-discharge measurements was three. Electrochemical 
impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was performed at 3.3 V. The measurement was conducted after the cell voltage was equal to 3.3 V 
during charging. The amplitude for the small signal input was 10 mV, and the measurement frequency ranged from 0.01 Hz to 7 
MHz. 
 
Results 
A. Structure of Composite Electrodes 
Fig. 2 shows the structures of the composite electrodes treated with WIP at various process temperatures. Figs. 2(a), (b), and (c) 
display the reconstructed CT images (upper) and the corresponding categorized composition images (lower) for RT, 100, and 150C, 
respectively. WIP was conducted at 600 MPa for all experiments. Note that the reconstructed images were displayed as the contrast 
was inverted from the case for normal X-ray imaging so that the distribution of AM can be legible and comparable with SEM images 
shown blow. Therefore, in this study, the material having lower transmittance (AM, SE, carbon-related materials, and voids in order) 
gives brighter grayscale tones. Comparing the cross-sections in the categorized images taken before WIP, shown in Fig. 2(d), the 
followings observations were made: First, an increase in the AM area (appearing green) was clearly observed after WIP treatment. 
Second, the SE area (red area) decreased simultaneously. Third, the portion of voids and carbon-related materials (black area) 
observed in the SE region (red area) nearly diminished, indicating that the electrodes were densified. The reduction of voids 
primarily occurred in the SE region, as the diameter of the SE particles was on the order of several microns, smaller than that for AM, 
which was very coarse after coating.

The proportion of voids/carbon region decreased with increasing process temperature. Fig. 3 summarizes the void ratio, determined 
as the ratio between the number of voxels for voids/carbon and those for all components. The resultant thickness of the composite 
electrodes as a function of processing temperature is shown on the right axis. Generally, both void ratio and thickness of the 
composite electrodes decreased with increasing process temperature. The thickness of the composite electrodes (as-fabricated value 
of 170 m) decreased monotonically from approximately 104 m to 94 m with process temperature. In contrast, the void ratio 
decreased at 100C and then showed a saturated trend at around 0.04 after the 150C WIP treatment. It is worth noting that the value 
of 0.04 means almost all voids were diminished within the resolution of the CT measurements, as the region contained both voids 
and carbon-related materials.

B. Electrochemical Performance 
Fig. 4 shows the charge-discharge performance of the test cells. The composite electrodes were pressurized with WIP at 600 MPa, at 
process temperatures of (a) RT, (b) 100, and (b) 150C. The specific capacity of the test cells increased with the process temperature, 
measuring approximately 110, 125, and 128 mAhg-1, respectively. Furthermore, the overpotential observed in the charge-discharge 
measurement curves decreased as the WIP temperature increased. The overpotential for the 150C cell was about 0.1 V lower than 
that for RT. Notably, the change was significant between the RT and the 100C treatments and relatively minor between 100 and the 
150C cells. The change suggests that charge-discharge performance correlates well with the reduction of voids in the SE, as shown 
in Fig. 3. 
The EIS results of the corresponding test cells are shown in Fig. 5. In the Nyquist plot, the real impedance versus the imaginary 
impedance [Fig.5(a)] features a symmetrical arc with a large offset from the origin in the coordinate system and then monotonously 
increases with a consistent slope. The frequency at the apex of the semicircle corresponds to the resistance. The arc is attributed to 
the resistance related to charge-transfer16). It was evident that the resistance between the interfaces decreased with increasing WIP 
temperature, while the Li-ion intercalation remained virtually unchanged. The offset from the origin on the horizontal axis ( 20 ) 
is due to the existence of bulk (Ohmic) resistance at the interface between the composite electrodes and the pellet-shaped SE and 
should be excluded from the present analysis. Similar trends are observed in the Bode plots shown in Fig. 5(b), where changes in R2 
are dominant. These observations conclude that higher-temperature WIP treatment significantly improves the interface properties 
between AM and the SE in the composite electrodes.

Discussion 
As discussed in the previous section, high-temperature WIP treatment significantly improves electrochemical properties. In addition, 
charge-discharging performance correlates well with the void proportion determined by CT measurements. To further explore the 
effect of process temperature on the electrochemical performance, the microstructures of the composite electrodes were examined 
using cross-sectional SEM. Fig. 6 shows the cross-section of the composite electrodes. Fig. 6(a) and (b) correspond to the 
cross-section of the electrode after WIP at RT and 190C, respectively. The cross-section of the electrode before WIP is also shown 
in Fig. 6(c) for comparison. It is evident from comparison with the cross-section before WIP that the WIP treatment at RT resulted in 
densification of the electrodes; however, most AM and SE particles remained isolated, with boundaries between adjacent AM 
similarly observed. In contrast, the cross-section of the 190C WIP electrode shows unclear boundaries and notable particle 
coalescence. In particular, the SE particles coalesced to form large particles without boundaries. The surface features after RT WIP 
treatment were similar to those obtained from the cross-section before WIP, suggesting that the high-temperature WIP enhanced the 
coalescence of both the AM and SE. The EDS results shown in Fig. 7 reveal that AM were replaced after the high-temperature WIP 
treatment. This implies a softening of the SE, resulting in increased fluidity and enhanced movement of particles during WIP.   
Fig. 8 shows the void ratio as a function of process duration. In this experiment, the pressure and temperature were set at 600 MPa 
and 100C to clarify the duration dependence on structural change. The void ratio drastically decreased immediately after pressing 
for 1 s and then gradually decreased, suggesting a two-step process. Fig. 9 shows a categorized composition image of the electrode 
with a WIP of 1 s. The electrode densified instantly, and the distribution of AM after a WIP of 1 s was similar to that for the longer 
case [see Fig.2(c), for example]. This indicates that densification was interrupted due to contact with each AM particle. The thickness 
of the electrode after 1 s WIP was 95 m, consistent with the 30 and 60 s samples, within the variation of sample preparation. It was 
concluded that the electrode densification was instantly achieved by WIP treatment. However, at this stage, many voids remained in 
the SE because the contact of the AM particles resulted in releasing applied pressure in the surroundings. Then, due to isostatic 
pressing, the voids gradually diminished with the movements of the AM and the SE particles increased. This gradual change can 
improve the electrochemical properties of the electrodes. To confirm this phenomenon, the mechanical properties of the SE should be 
clarified, which will be an extension of the present work.

Conclusions 
The densification mechanism during WIP and the correlation between the microstructure and battery performance were investigated. 
X-ray CT observations revealed that in the composite electrodes processed at 600 MPa for 60 s, both the void ratio and the thickness 
of the electrode decreased with increasing process temperature. Charge-discharge performance showed that as the WIP temperature 
increased, the overpotential decreased and the specific capacity increased, implying a correction with the void ratio. EIS showed that 
the resistance related to charge transfer decreased with increasing WIP temperature, indicating the formation of an excellent interface 
between AM and SE. The duration dependence of the structural changes suggests two process steps. The enhanced movement of AM 
and SE particles could lead to improved electrochemical properties of the electrodes.
